summary: New team members are setting up Jira automation rules for this repo, but the only documentation in the repository is a single-line README. They don't have anywhere to look up which events to send from Jira, what payload fields those events need, or which GitHub secrets and runners have to be in place for the automation to actually run.

Two automation workflows already exist and work today: a 'work order' step that reviews a new ticket and writes a structured plan back to it, and a 'build' step that implements an approved ticket and opens a draft pull request. Each is triggered by a specific Jira automation rule firing a GitHub event, and each depends on specific secrets and a self-hosted runner — none of that is written down anywhere outside the workflow YAML itself.

Done means README.md has a clear, scannable section for each of the two workflows covering what triggers it, what it does end to end, and what must be configured (runner, secrets) for it to work — enough for someone setting up or troubleshooting a Jira automation rule to get the event name and payload right without having to read the YAML. No workflow, prompt, or script files change; the page should stay roughly one page long.
clarifications: 'Each one' is read as the two automation workflows that exist in the repo today: .github/workflows/agent-work-order.yml (Stage 1, work order generation) and .github/workflows/agent-build.yml (Stage 2, implementation and PR). There is no third workflow to document.

'What needs to be configured' is read as three things per workflow: the required GitHub repository secrets, the self-hosted runner label(s) it targets, and the repository_dispatch event name plus payload fields the Jira automation rule must send.
'Roughly one page' is treated as a soft length target — favor completeness on the two workflows over trimming further if something has to give.
important_details: The two workflows target different runner labels: agent-work-order.yml requires [self-hosted, claude], while agent-build.yml only requires self-hosted. Worth calling out explicitly so whoever provisions runners doesn't assume one runner satisfies both.
agent-work-order.yml can also be triggered manually via workflow_dispatch with a ticket_key input, separate from the Jira-driven repository_dispatch path — useful for re-running a stuck ticket.

agent-work-order.yml hardcodes Jira status and label names (Work Order, Intake, needs-details, etc.) in its env block that must stay in sync with the Jira project's workflow and automation rules; the README should mention that dependency exists even without enumerating every value.
This is documentation-only: do not modify agent-work-order.yml, agent-build.yml, or anything under .github/agents/ — describe current behavior as-is.

acceptance_criteria: README.md has a section for agent-work-order.yml covering: its trigger (work-order-requested repository_dispatch, plus manual workflow_dispatch with ticket_key), what a run does (fetches the ticket from Jira, has Claude review it read-only, writes back either a formatted work order or a needs-details bounce to Intake), and what must be configured (self-hosted runner with the claude label; secrets JIRA_DOMAIN, JIRA_EMAIL, JIRA_API_TOKEN).

README.md has a section for agent-build.yml covering: its trigger (jira-plan-approved repository_dispatch with ticket_key, summary, description payload fields), what a run does (Claude implements the change on a new agent/<ticket_key> branch, opens a draft PR against main, and a comment with the PR link is posted back to the Jira ticket), and what must be configured (self-hosted runner; contents:write and pull-requests:write permissions; secrets JIRA_DOMAIN, JIRA_EMAIL, JIRA_API_TOKEN).
Only README.md is changed — no workflow YAML, prompt, schema, or script file under .github is touched.
The result reads as roughly one page: a short shared-pipeline intro plus one scannable subsection per workflow, not a line-by-line YAML walkthrough.
out_of_scope: Writing or changing the Jira automation rules themselves — this documents the GitHub-side contract (event names, payload, secrets) those rules must satisfy; configuring the rules in Jira is separate work for whoever owns that project.
File-by-file documentation of the shared helper scripts (.github/agents/lib/jira.sh, adf.jq) or the prompt/schema files — the README should describe workflow-level behavior, not the internal helpers.
Any change to trigger names, secrets, runner labels, or workflow logic — this ticket documents current behavior only.

codebase.relevance: Stage 1 workflow: header comment already summarizes the pipeline; on:/env: blocks give the trigger event, ticket_key input, and the WORK_ORDER_STATUS/INTAKE_STATUS/secret names to document.
Stage 2 workflow: on:/permissions:/env: blocks give the jira-plan-approved event, its payload fields, and the secrets and write permissions needed to open a PR and comment back on Jira.
Shows exactly which Jira REST calls and secrets (JIRA_DOMAIN, JIRA_EMAIL, JIRA_API_TOKEN) both workflows depend on — useful as the source of truth for the secrets list.
Describes what Claude is asked to do in Stage 1 at a high level — useful for summarizing 'what it does' without quoting it verbatim.
Currently a single line ('# jira-github-workflow-testing' / 'Testing Jira to GitHub workflows'); this is the file to expand.

resources.summary: Explains how repository_dispatch triggers a workflow and the client_payload shape — directly relevant since both workflows are triggered this way from Jira.

resources.topic: GitHub Actions self-hosted runners and labels
resources.summary: Explains how runs-on label matching works, relevant because the two workflows target different label sets ([self-hosted, claude] vs self-hosted) and that distinction needs to be clear to whoever provisions runners.
How repository secrets like JIRA_API_TOKEN are created and referenced from a workflow — relevant to the 'what needs to be configured' half of the ask.

How a Jira automation rule fires the repository_dispatch webhook GitHub expects — the piece new team members are actually configuring, so framing the README from this angle will make it more useful to them.

getting_started: Read both workflow files top to bottom once — they're short, and the header comment in agent-work-order.yml already frames the two-stage pipeline; that framing is a good starting point for the README.

Open with a short 'pipeline' paragraph (ticket created → work order generated → plan approved → build/PR opened) before the per-workflow sections, since that's the context a Jira rule author needs first.

For each workflow, pull the trigger event name and payload fields straight from its on: block and the required secrets from its env:/secrets usage — no need to trace every step, just enough to describe input, output, and configuration.
A small table (trigger event, payload fields, runner label, required secrets) per workflow may be the most scannable way to fit both within roughly one page.

confidence.reason: The two workflows are short and self-contained, so extracting trigger/secrets/runner details is straightforward, but 'roughly one page' is a soft target and the workflows differ enough (runner labels, payload shape, permissions) that some judgment is needed to stay concise without omitting a real configuration difference.

customer_data.reason: This is internal documentation about CI/CD trigger and secret configuration; no customer data is read, written, or referenced.

open_questions: Should the README also explain how to configure the Jira automation rules themselves (rule name, 'Send web request' setup), or stay strictly on the GitHub-side trigger/secrets/runner contract? Best answered by whoever owns the Jira automation rules.
Is there an existing internal doc for provisioning the self-hosted runner(s) that the README should link to, or should basic runner setup be described here as well?
